newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico, Texas sign anti-money laundering pact.
newsitem.headline: Mexico, Texas sign anti-money laundering pact.

text.p: Mexico and the U.S. state of Texas on Tuesday signed an agreement to join forces in hitting drug traffickers where it hurts most -- on the profit margin.
Texas and Mexico, which share 1,200 miles (1,900 km) of border, pledged to work together to combat money laundering, the system by which drug traffickers falsely account for their mostly cash income.

Texas Attorney General Dan Morales and Mexico's anti-drug Commissioner Francisco Molina Ruiz signed the agreement, which among other things will designate Mexican representatives in Texas as official liaisons with Texas authorities.
In addition, the Texas Anti-Money Laundering Task Force under Morales's domain will communicate directly with Mexico.
"I recognize it is somewhat uncommon for a federal office of one country to work jointly with a state office in another government," Morales told reporters after appearing jointly with Molina.
"But I think ... the Mexican government ... is more concerned about attacking problems than respecting the niceties and all of the technicalities of protocol," Morales said.

Morales, ending a two-day visit to Mexico on Tuesday, said the recent move toward cooperation meant that officials on both sides of the border were only now catching up on years of neglect by failing to work together.

In addition, he said the United States and Mexico faced greater challenges in stemming the drug trade over the next several years as the remaining trade barriers between the two countries are phased out under the North American Free Trade Agreement.

"As those barriers are lowered and as trade restrictions are relaxed we must anticipate that given the recent advances in technology ... and the ability to transfer cash instantaneously that it will be that much more difficult for us to detect and investigate," Morales said.

But the fight can be won, Morales said, citing a recent Texas and U.S. federal crackdown on 74 wire transfer houses in and around Houston that he said were used to launder more than $89 million in drug money on its way to Colombia.
After arrests were made and the houses closed down, money transfers from Houston to Colombia plummeted 70 percent, Morales said.
